chapter: Conspiracy, Recovery of Dapple, Slaying a Giant, and Home Again

facts: Chapter 7 opens, titled Conspiracy, Recovery of Dapple, Slaying a Giant, and Home Again
Sancho took the high road for Toboso
The next day he sighted the inn where they had tossed him in a blanket
As he looked at it fearfully, he saw two men come out whom he recognized at once as the priest and the barber from his native village
These two friends of Don Quixote were in fact searching for the poor gentleman
When they saw Sancho they demanded an account of his master, whose horse he was riding
After hesitating, Sancho began to tell them
A half-page engraving sits at the top, captioned with Sancho finding him at last in a rocky recess
Sancho told the priest and the barber the whole story of their adventures, where his master was, and what he was about
That night they remained at the inn and considered the best means of getting the knight back to his house
They came to the conclusion that the most promising plan was to lure him away by pretending that the Lady Dulcinea had commanded his presence at Toboso
They instructed Sancho carefully in the part he was to play in carrying it out
On the following day Sancho started off to return to his knight
The priest and the barber would follow at a more leisurely pace
Once in the mountains the squire hunted for his master and found him at last in a rocky recess
Don Quixote had his clothes on and his armor hanging from the branch of a tree
The knight was surprised to see him so soon, but immediately began asking him questions about his mission to Dulcinea
Sancho's powers of invention were severely strained, but he had a good deal of natural ingenuity and had been well coached by the priest and barber in what to say
He said at once, truthfully, that in his haste to leave he had forgotten the letter Don Quixote had written to Dulcinea
Indeed, two days after he left, the knight had found the letter still in the pocketbook
Sancho said that because he remembered the message so well he had not returned for the letter
The rest of his story had nothing to do with the truth
He told his master he had repeated the contents of the letter to a parish clerk in a place he came to, who wrote it down, and that he took it on to Toboso
Don Quixote said he had no doubt Sancho found his Queen of Beauty in a stately apartment stringing pearls on gold thread
Sancho answered no, that he found her winnowing bushels of wheat in her father's backyard
He said that when he offered her the letter she told him to put it down until her hands were free, and that while he waited he helped her move sacks
Don Quixote said that surely then he perceived a fragrance, a perfume like that of a fancy shop

glossary.winnowing: Separating kernels of wheat from their shells, called chaff, by tossing it in the air and allowing the wind to blow the chaff away.

facts: Sancho answered that she smelled pretty strong, and that he thought it was garlic and onions, though she was sweating hard from the work so it is hard to know
He said that when she stopped working she picked up the letter and ripped it up
His explanation was that she can neither read nor write and did not want her secret to become known by asking anybody to read the letter to her
He said he told her all about his master's love for her, and that she said she would a thousand times rather see him than read the letter
He reported her order that Don Quixote leave off his pranks among the rocks and briars
He said he asked her whether a Biscayan fellow had come to her, and she said one had, but she knew nothing of Gines de Pasamonte or the galley slaves
Don Quixote supposed she had given him a jewel when he departed
Sancho answered that all she gave him was a piece of bread and cheese
Don Quixote said he would go to her at once in obedience to her command, which was just what Sancho wanted to hear
The knight said there was only one thing he did not understand: it is more than thirty leagues from there to Toboso, yet Sancho had only been journeying three days to there and back
Sancho, blushing, said he could not understand it himself and thought there must be magic in it, since Rocinante flew like the wind

glossary.leagues: A league is a measure of distance that ranges from 2.5 to 4 miles.

facts: A half-page engraving sits at the top, captioned with the fat squire unhappily trudging along on foot
Don Quixote said that was it, and that it often happens that a friendly magician will enable a knight to get over a thousand leagues in a day
The knight rode on Rocinante, talking about this subject, while the fat squire unhappily trudged alongside on foot
As they went they came upon the priest and the barber
The priest and the barber were pretending to be travellers at rest on the roadside
Sancho had been looking for them anxiously and was glad now to be free from the responsibility of telling more lies
Don Quixote recognized them at once and got down to greet them
The priest said that he and their friend master Nicholas, the barber, were going to Seville to collect an inheritance of sixty thousand crowns left to him by a relative in India
He said that the day before they were attacked by four highwaymen who stripped them of everything worth taking
He said the thieves were said to be part of a gang of galley slaves set free in that region by a man valiant enough to overcome their guards, and mad enough to let loose such a pack of wolves
Don Quixote hung down his head at these words
Sancho cried out that in truth it was his master who did that job

Don Quixote said angrily that if he did, it is because it is a knight's duty to help the distressed and suffering, and that he was prepared to make good this principle against anyone with his spear and sword
No one present would accept the challenge and so they walked on in silence
Sancho was plodding along wearily, full of regrets over his lost Dapple, when they saw a man on a gray donkey coming towards them
A single glance convinced Sancho that the man was riding the donkey he had just been thinking about
A second look satisfied him that the rider was no other than the bandit Gines de Pasamonte disguised as a gypsy
The thief was just as quick to perceive the danger he had unexpectedly fallen into, and he jumped down and ran off at a speed that made pursuit hopeless
Sancho ran to Dapple and, with many endearing words, kissed her and hugged her neck as if she had been a lost child
Mounted on her again, Sancho felt a new joy in life and thought no more of his recent troubles and discomforts
Late in the afternoon of the next day the party reached the inn where the blanket-tossing incident occurred
Little was said of that topic after the innkeeper was assured that all charges would be paid this time
Don Quixote retired early, being overly fatigued, and soon fell into a feverish sleep
The rest of the party, as well as other guests, stayed up very late talking and telling stories

They were nearly finished when Sancho burst in among them and cried out with great dismay that his master was in a desperate battle with an enormous giant, whose head he had sheared off his shoulders as clean as a turnip, with blood running everywhere
They could now hear Don Quixote shouting at a scoundrel that he could not escape and that his scimitar would not save him
Then came the sound of blows against the walls
The innkeeper said he hoped the knight had not interfered with the wine-bags hanging near his bed
With that the whole company made for the knight's room
The first thing they saw was Don Quixote standing in his shirt, with a little red nightcap on his head and a blanket over his left arm, slashing with his sword all around him
The landlord's fears proved true: the room was flooded with wine from the gashed wine-bags
The landlord lunged for Don Quixote, who seemed to be sleepwalking, but others kept him from harming the knight
The barber threw a bucket of water on Don Quixote to awaken him, but it hardly seemed to bring him to his senses
Sancho declared that he had seen the giant and went looking for its head, and not finding it he said the inn was enchanted

The landlord demanded whether Sancho could not see this was nothing but wine from the ripped-up skins, and swore neither he nor his crazy master would escape this time without paying every penny of the damages

glossary.scimitar: A saber with a curved blade, mainly used by the Turks and Arabs.

facts: A half-page engraving sits at the top, captioned with Don Quixote slashing with his sword all around him
The priest calmed the innkeeper and his family down, promising that all the wines and skins would be paid for
Don Quixote, who still was in a state of fever, was put back to bed under Sancho's care, and peace ruled the inn again
It was several days before the knight was well enough to resume the homeward journey
He now made that journey stretched out in an ox cart hired for the purpose
It was noon on Sunday when the party reached the village
Everybody, especially the niece and housekeeper, was shocked to see how pale and thin and weak the knight was
While Don Quixote was being carried into the house to be put to bed, Sancho's wife Teresa came out to greet him
First she asked about Dapple's health and satisfied herself by looking over the donkey
Then she turned to her husband and asked him what profit he had to show for deserting his family
Her ruffled temper was smoothed when she learned that he had come home with a hundred gold crowns, plus the wages he earned from the trip
As for the glory he claimed from it, she thought as little of that as she did of the prospect of being the governor of an island
Many days later, when Don Quixote's health was improved and he and Sancho had been talking together, Sancho came home in such a cheery mood that his wife asked what made him so pleased
Sancho answered that he was so well pleased that he would be more pleased if it pleased God that he was less pleased than he is pleased
Teresa said she did not understand him and asked how one can be pleased not to be pleased
Sancho explained that he is pleased to return to the service of Don Quixote, who desires to go on adventures for a third time, and that he wishes to come across another hundred crowns if possible
He said he is sorry to part from her and the children, for if he could live at home at ease it would be better than tramping the roads
Sancho finished his thought: tramping around on rough roads is why he says he would be better pleased if God pleased that he was not so pleased to go
Teresa said that ever since he went knight-erranting he talks in such a roundabout way that nobody can understand him
Sancho said it is enough that God understands him
He told her to take special care now of Dapple and see that she is in good condition and the pack saddle in good order

He said they shall have to endure many hardships, many giants and dragons and evil spirits, and hissings and roarings and bellowings and bleatings, not to mention enchanted Moors, who are worse than all the rest together
He said his only hope is for an island where he can live without trouble or danger
Teresa asked why he cannot do without an island, and told him to do what he pleases and not bother her with his speeches
She added that if he is determined to be a governor, he should take their son Sancho with him and bring him up to the business
Sancho said he will send for the boy with plenty of money for his expenses, and that as for their daughter Mary Sancho, she shall be a countess
Teresa said to send money for the boy, but that as for Mary she shall think of her as being as good as dead the day she becomes a countess
Teresa finished her answer, saying he should do what he pleases, for wives must obey their husbands even when they are blockheads
On that parting shot, Sancho returned to his master
Don Quixote was just then talking earnestly with Sampson Carrasco, a young friend and neighbor who had recently finished his studies at the University of Salamanca
The young man was telling Don Quixote that his fame had spread far and wide, and in turn listening to his views on knight-errantry
Carrasco's idea in all this was weaning Don Quixote from his delusions, or at least keeping him safe at home
He could think of no better treatment than one based on the very folly of the knight
So, far from opposing the plan for a new expedition, he was encouraging it
His advice was a surprise to the knight, and more so to the niece and housekeeper, who had supposed Carrasco would do his best to oppose the madness of their master
Three days later Don Quixote and Sancho sallied forth again
The knight had a new helmet supplied by Carrasco, who insisted on escorting them well beyond the village
